section: 1 Introduction
text: Watermarking and fingerprinting constitute the foundational technical infrastructure for securing large language models (LLMs) across their full lifecycle—from pretraining data provenance and fine-tuning lineage to API-mediated deployment and edge-device adaptation—yet they remain conceptually and operationally distinct from broader AI safety, privacy, and robustness paradigms.

section: 1 Introduction
rationale: [1] proposes safety guardrails for LLM outputs; [2],[3] review privacy techniques against membership inference and data leakage. The watermark/fingerprint characterization (main clause) is uncited survey framing, so AutoSurvey joint is No.
text: Unlike safety guardrails that constrain harmful outputs or privacy-preserving mechanisms that mitigate membership inference or data leakage, watermarking and fingerprinting are *provenance-first* primitives: they encode verifiable claims of origin, ownership, or usage into either model behavior or its artifacts, enabling forensic accountability without altering functional intent.

text: This distinction is critical: while alignment techniques optimize for human values and differential privacy enforces statistical indistinguishability, watermarking and fingerprinting enforce *traceability*—a property increasingly mandated by regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act’s transparency obligations and U.S. copyright litigation landscapes.

text: Crucially, these pressures expose a fundamental asymmetry: watermarking is *active*, owner-controlled embedding of secret-key–dependent signals into outputs or parameters, whereas fingerprinting is *passive*, forensic identification of intrinsic behavioral or structural signatures—such as activation sparsity patterns, attention manifold geometry, or latent-space confusion zones —without requiring prior coordination.

section: 2.1 Tripartite Embedding Locus Taxonomy: Output, Parameter, and Behavior Spaces
text: The tripartite embedding locus taxonomy—output, parameter, and behavior spaces—constitutes the ontological bedrock upon which all watermarking and fingerprinting paradigms for large language models must be rigorously grounded.

rationale: Justifies the survey's own locus-based taxonomy.
text: Unlike implementation-centric taxonomies that fragment techniques by algorithmic family (e.g., sampling-based vs. cryptographic), this functional classification centers on *where provenance information is physically instantiated*, thereby exposing first-principles constraints on stealth, persistence, adversarial resilience, and deployment feasibility.

section: 2.2 Detection Modality Spectrum: From White-Box Verification to Black-Box Auditing
rationale: Survey's framing of the detection-modality axis.
text: The detection modality spectrum constitutes a foundational axis of operational security in watermarking and fingerprinting—defining not *what* is verified, but *how much* the verifier knows about the model’s internals.

section: 2.2 Detection Modality Spectrum: From White-Box Verification to Black-Box Auditing
rationale: Survey's own three-tier definition of white/gray/black-box detection.
text: We formalize this as a three-tiered continuum: white-box (full parameter access), gray-box (intermediate representations—logits, attention maps, or architectural priors), and black-box (query-response behavior only)—each imposing distinct constraints on adversary capability, verification latency, forensic rigor, and real-world deployability.

section: 2.3 Formal Security Properties: A Unified Information-Theoretic and Cryptographic Framework
rationale: Meta statement of what the subsection does.
text: This subsection establishes a unifying formal framework that transcends heuristic claims of “robustness” or “stealth” by axiomatizing four interdependent security properties—detectability, robustness, unforgeability, and collusion resistance—through the complementary lenses of information theory, cryptography, and game-theoretic adversarial modeling.

section: 2.3 Formal Security Properties: A Unified Information-Theoretic and Cryptographic Framework
rationale: [39] revisits prior theoretical work arguing random-walk attacks can erase any watermark given quality and perturbation oracles, and finds mixing slow and oracles unreliable, so watermarks are far more robust in practice.
text: Crucially, these properties are not independent; their simultaneous satisfaction is constrained by fundamental limits exposed in seminal impossibility results, which prove that no watermark can be both *strongly robust* (i.e., resistant to quality-preserving perturbations) and *computationally undetectable* without degrading output fidelity—a consequence of the attacker’s access to a quality oracle and a perturbation oracle inducing an efficiently mixing walk over high-quality outputs.

section: 2.3 Formal Security Properties: A Unified Information-Theoretic and Cryptographic Framework
text: Detectability is formally grounded in statistical hypothesis testing: the null hypothesis $H_0$ posits that text is drawn from the unwatermarked model distribution $\mathcal{P}_0$, while the alternative $H_1$ asserts it originates from the watermarked distribution $\mathcal{P}_1$.

section: 2.4 Threat Model Taxonomy: Adversary Capabilities, Goals, and Attack Surfaces
rationale: Meta bridge sentence between subsections.
text: A rigorous threat model taxonomy is indispensable for unifying the fragmented landscape of watermarking and fingerprinting security analysis—and serves as the essential bridge between the formal security properties established in the preceding subsection and the paradigm-convergent design principles introduced in the following one.

section: 2.4 Threat Model Taxonomy: Adversary Capabilities, Goals, and Attack Surfaces
text: Rather than treating attacks as isolated phenomena, we formalize a three-axis orthogonal classification—adversary capability (access modality), operational goal (intent), and attack surface (locus of intervention)—that exposes deep structural symmetries across paradigms and reveals systemic vulnerabilities masked by siloed evaluation.

rationale: [39] studies quality-preserving random-walk removal attacks and finds them weak in practice; [50] shows out-of-distribution trigger sets make backdoor watermarks vulnerable to white-box erasure.
text: This taxonomy directly operationalizes the impossibility constraints and detection-robustness trade-offs articulated earlier: for instance, the fundamental distortion–robustness tension manifests most acutely in output-space removal attacks, while the vulnerability of backdoor-based schemes to out-of-distribution triggers reflects a failure to satisfy the *unforgeability* and *collusion resistance* axioms under white-box neutralization intent.

section: 8 Conclusion
rationale: [108] proposes ZKPs for LLM data verification and access control; [66] records the LLM data supply chain on a blockchain; [121] surveys evaluation of generative-AI harms. Forensic admissibility and register-level perceptual evaluation are absent.
text: Future work must therefore co-design watermarking with system-level governance: integrating zero-knowledge proofs for forensic admissibility, blockchain-anchored provenance trails, and human-centered evaluation protocols that quantify perceptual fidelity disparities across linguistic registers.

section: 8 Conclusion
text: Only through such interdisciplinary integration can watermarking and fingerprinting evolve from fragile technical add-ons into verifiable, equitable, and legally enforceable pillars of AI accountability.
